research_claims.claim: **A production ML system is mostly not the model.** The authors state that a model usually contains only about five per cent of the code required to put an ML application into production.

**Production ML differs from research ML on data, priorities and lifetime.** Research ML uses a static dataset, one design priority and a single terminal result; production ML uses shifting real-world data, several competing priorities, and continuous monitoring, assessment and retraining.

**Training data must cover the feature space of the prediction requests the system will actually receive**, and coverage density matters as much as example count because duplicated or near-duplicated examples add no information.
**Encoding ambiguity is a data defect with the same status as a missing value.** The authors' example is an elevation reading of zero that may mean sea level or may mean that no measurement arrived.
**Where one model's output is another model's input, errors propagate over time**, which makes upstream model monitoring a dependency of downstream model correctness.

**Drift and skew are different comparisons and should not be conflated.** Drift compares successive iterations of one data source over time; skew compares two different sources, characteristically training against serving.

**Data drift is a change in the distribution of the input features; concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and labels.** Concept drift invalidates the mapping the model learned rather than merely moving the inputs.
**Skew decomposes into schema skew, feature skew and distribution skew**, which are detected by different mechanisms and have different remedies.

**The rate at which ground truth changes determines the labelling strategy.** Change over months or years permits crowd-based curated datasets; change over days or hours forces direct feedback or weak supervision.

**Training–serving skew is caused by performing different preprocessing at training and at serving**, and the authors describe it as a common production failure that is hard to detect because the model continues to return plausible answers.

**The structural remedy for training–serving skew is to export the preprocessing as a graph and attach it to the served model**, so that full-pass statistics computed once at training are applied element-wise at serving by the same code.

**Transformations divide into instance-level and full-pass**, and only the former can be computed from a single serving request, so full-pass results must be stored as constants and shipped with the model.

**Aggregate metrics conceal subgroup failure, and which slices matter is a domain-knowledge question rather than a statistical one.** Slicing on metadata the model does not consume can be more informative than slicing on model features.

**ML systems are sensitive in two ways ordinary software tests do not catch: entanglement, where changing one feature changes the whole model, and configuration, where a small error in hyperparameters, versions or feature lists silently changes behaviour.**

**Observability in ML is imported from control theory, where a system can only be controlled to the extent that it can be observed**, and is operationalised through alertability, meaning metrics and thresholds that make failure unambiguous, and actionability, meaning enough signal to support root cause analysis.

**Monitoring splits into functional monitoring of predictive performance and serving-data distributions, and non-functional monitoring of latency, failures and resource use**, and the second matters independently of the first because a system that is down serves no predictions at all.

**Drift detection splits into supervised techniques that require fresh labels and unsupervised techniques that do not**, the latter being the practical default because labelling is slow and expensive.

**Retraining policy is a design decision with no correct answer.** The authors report that scheduled retraining is common because it is simple and often adequate, while noting that it assumes a steady rate of change in the world which frequently does not hold.
**Latency, throughput and cost trade against each other and against accuracy**, and the authors state as a general rule that shorter latency costs more.

**For online serving, latency rather than accuracy is usually the binding requirement**, so a simpler model that clears the accuracy bar is preferred to a more accurate model that does not clear the latency bar.

**Model complexity should be added against a fixed serving infrastructure and a declared gating metric**, so that complexity stops when an operational constraint such as latency or model size is breached rather than when improvement stops.

**Optimisation techniques trade accuracy for resource cost, and the size of the loss is specific to the model and data and hard to predict in advance.** Quantisation, pruning and knowledge distillation each reduce size or latency at some accuracy cost that must be measured rather than assumed.

**Neural networks do learn to suppress uninformative features, but the suppressed capacity is still stored, still traversed at inference and still requires the feature to be collected and maintained for the life of the product.**

**MLOps extends DevOps in two specific ways: continuous integration must validate data, schemas and models rather than only code, and continuous delivery ships a pipeline that produces a prediction service rather than shipping a model.**
**The authors describe MLOps maturity as levels 0, 1 and 2 defined by how much of the workflow is automated**, and mark level 2 as still somewhat speculative at the time of writing.
**There is no industry-standard scheme for versioning models.** The authors propose a major, minor and pipeline scheme and describe several incompatible alternatives in current use.

**Lineage is what makes a model reproducible, comparable across runs, and deletable on request.** Recording artefacts, executions and contexts turns provenance questions into queries rather than investigations.

**Live experimentation exists because model metrics are not business metrics.** A recommender trained to maximise click-through is optimising a labelled proxy for a profit objective that was never in the training data.
**Equal fairness metrics across groups do not establish that a system is fair**, and fairness evaluation must be repeated through development and after launch rather than treated as a release gate.

**Interpretability has no mathematical definition and is not cleanly separable from explainability**, so the working definition the authors adopt requires only that a human can understand the model's operations through introspection or a produced explanation.
**Privacy costs accuracy, computation time, or both**, and the cheapest control is not collecting the data in the first place.
**A deletion request may force a retrain**, which makes data and model lineage a precondition for satisfying data-protection obligations rather than an optional engineering nicety.
**Pipeline orchestration is required because components have ordering dependencies and because expensive completed steps must be cached so that a failure reruns only the failing component.**
**Not every project needs a pipeline.** Pipelines are unnecessary for pure experimentation and become necessary once a model has users and therefore requires continuous update.

**The book's closing position is to reason about ML systems rather than ML models**, the diagnostic questions being how users interact with the model, whether they can report misclassifications, and whether that feedback reaches retraining.
Observe activity where it occurs; do not substitute requested features or generalized self-report for design data.
Interpret with the person and then again with the cross-functional team.
Consolidate inductively before claiming population patterns.
Use multiple models because each representation reveals and hides different structure.
Keep ideas visibly connected to evidence through the Wall Walk.
Generate several visions before converging on product concepts.
Alternate scenario thinking and structural thinking throughout detailed design.
Define places and purposes before widgets; define interface architecture before visual detail.
Treat every design as a hypothesis and prototypes as instruments for discovering where it fails.
Resolve validation findings from practice to product structure to interaction structure to interface detail.
Slice releases by coherent user value, then prioritize function within the slice.
Keep the user-facing architecture available to implementation teams so local decisions preserve the whole.
The thesis is two sentences: focus on the domain and domain logic; base complex domain designs on a model.
Two practices are **prerequisites**, not recommendations: iterative development, and a continuing close relationship between developers and domain experts.
Knowledge crunching is joint modelling under correction, led by developers; it is not requirements elicitation.
The engineer's goal is not to become a domain expert but to "talk to experts, understand the major concepts relevant to the application, and sanity-check what we were building."
The ubiquitous language exists to eliminate translation, because translation creates bilingual bottlenecks whose "translations are inexact."
The language is the customer's jargon **cleaned up** — sharper and narrower — with the experts holding a veto if the cleaning distorts accepted field meaning.
A change to the language is a change to the model, and must ripple into the code.
Speaking scenarios aloud is a first-class modelling technique; "Rough edges are easy to hear."
Sophisticated domain experts must understand the core of the model; technical components are explicitly exempt.
Multiple dialects are expected; the division that must never exist is between experts and developers.
Model-driven design requires a modelling paradigm with tool support and has "limited applicability" in purely procedural languages.
Anyone contributing to the model must touch the code; specialised roles remain legitimate.
Aggregates are consistency boundaries with a single root controlling all access, making it practical to enforce invariants on every state change.
Deep models arrive through many small refactorings punctuated by occasional breakthroughs; a breakthrough "is not a technique; it is an event."
Never adopt a model a domain expert would not use, however elegant it seems.
Total model unification across a large enterprise "will not be feasible or cost-effective."
A bounded context is bounded in team organisation, application usage and physical artefacts — not merely in namespaces; a module is not a context.
Duplicate concepts and false cognates are the two failure signatures inside a context.
Context maps describe reality first; "don't change the map until the change in reality is done."
Context boundaries follow team and political contours as much as technical ones.
Conformity to a good upstream model is chosen "less often than we probably should" and can drag you into a better design.
An anticorruption layer translates concepts, not messages, and its isolation must be costed.
Non-integration is a legitimate, often correct, answer.
The core domain is relative to point of view, cannot usually be purchased, should be made small, and should get the best people.
Generic subdomains should not be designed for reuse.
Large-scale structure must evolve; imposing it up front is likely to be costly.
Strategic design requires minimalism and humility, and architecture teams must not absorb all the strongest people.
**Change the game:** reject the false choice between hard positional pressure and soft concession.
**Two-level diagnosis:** keep substantive issues distinct from relationship and process issues; negotiate both on their merits.
**Perception before persuasion:** reconstruct the choice and consequences as the other side sees them.
**Interests behind positions:** ask why and why not; list multiple material, relational, identity, and constituent interests.
**Concrete flexibility:** state interests precisely while treating any particular solution as revisable.
**Invent before deciding:** use explicit no-commitment option generation, then improve and evaluate candidates later.
**Dovetail differences:** trade across forecasts, valuations, timing, risk, scope, and priorities rather than split one number.
**Make their decision easy:** design an agreement the counterpart can implement and explain to constituents.
**Objective criteria and fair procedures:** reason from standards independent of either side's will; examine competing standards rather than invoking “fairness” as a slogan.
**BATNA:** develop and select the best action available without agreement; compare packages against it.
**Trip wire:** predefine a threshold that forces reassessment before a poor agreement is accepted.
**Micro-BATNA:** prepare what to do if this meeting ends without agreement.
**Negotiation jujitsu:** redirect positions, criticism, and personal attack into questions about interests, options, and standards.
**Questions and silence:** use inquiry to surface reasoning, then leave room for an answer.
**One-text procedure:** iterate one draft through criticism when competing proposals cause positional lock-in.
**Negotiate the process:** name suspected tactics, test them, and agree rules before proceeding.
**Framework agreement:** expose unresolved terms early and draft toward operational commitments.
**Seven sources of power:** relationship, communication/process, interests, options, legitimacy, BATNA, and commitment.
**Question quality is owned by the interviewer.** Socially generous respondents are a predictable condition, not an excuse for weak evidence.
**Facts before opinions.** Recent episodes, actual workflows, current costs, prior attempts, and allocated resources are more useful than approval or prediction.
**Importance before detail.** Establish that the problem category is active and consequential before ranking needs inside it.
**Problem ownership and solution ownership differ.** Stakeholders supply evidence about their lives; the product team remains responsible for design judgement.
**Deflect, anchor, dig.** Redirect compliments, ground generic and future claims in past specifics, and investigate the cause beneath requests and emotions.
**Expose the dangerous assumption.** Ask what would cause failure and what must be true for success; include legal, budget, adoption, distribution, and technical dependencies.
**Choose the evidence mechanism by risk.** Conversation can investigate market and customer uncertainty; product risk requires prototypes, technical spikes, usage, or other direct tests.
**Commitment is costly behaviour.** Interpret time, reputation, and money relative to what the particular stakeholder is actually sacrificing.
**Advancement needs a named next state.** A warm meeting without a decision, owner, condition, or next action is not pipeline progress.
**Segmentation makes evidence comparable.** Mixed answers across unlike populations should not be aggregated as one customer voice.
**A useful segment is findable.** Pair a specific kind of person or organisation with the place or behaviour through which they can be reached.
**Learning is a team state.** Shared preparation, first-hand exposure, retrievable notes, and immediate review prevent one person becoming the repository of customer truth.
**Speed means resolving the next uncertainty.** The three-question list changes as beliefs change; conversations stop when they cease adding relevant information.
Change happens one person at a time; "Successful change, at its core, is rooted in something much simpler: How to facilitate change with one person."
The five elements are building blocks: "All five elements must be in place for a change to be realized", and they "must occur in sequence and they are cumulative."
The ordering argument is **entailment, not evidence** — desire cannot precede awareness, knowledge cannot precede desire, and so on down the chain.
The model "begins after a change has been identified" and says nothing about whether the change is right.
Awareness covers the nature of the change, the reason for it, the risk of not changing, the internal and external drivers, **and** "what's in it for me" — it is not only the *why*.
Communicating is not the same as producing awareness: "Awareness is not achieved based on the messages sent, but rather how the messages are received and internalized by each person."
Reception is governed by five factors, of which contestability of the stated reasons is the one teams most often ignore.
Desire is "ultimately about personal choice" and "by definition, not under our direct control"; assuming it follows from awareness is the named executive error.
The correct first move against resistance is to identify the barrier point, then "stop talking and start listening".
Knowledge is not the starting point; training aimed past an awareness or desire barrier does not work.
Knowledge is not ability: ability is "turning knowledge into action" at "the required performance levels", and some people never reach it.
Ability requires practice, time, coaching, obstacle removal and "a safe environment to practice new skills and job roles".
An unopened feedback channel makes a broken system look like a failing employee.
Reinforcement must be meaningful, tied to real accomplishment, free of countervailing consequences, and backed by accountability in day-to-day operations.
The barrier point is "the first element of the model that is weak or would be assessed as 'low'" — operationally, the first element scoring 3 or below on an anonymous 1–5 self-rating.

Hiatt's own statements about effort past the barrier are conditional ("will not by itself", "will not be productive until"), with one absolute exception: "In the absence of desire, no amount of knowledge can produce change."
The model is offered as a lens over existing practice, not as a replacement for it, and explicitly not as a prescribed process.
The elements apply to customers, suppliers, the public and school communities, not only to employees.
The eight errors are the diagnosis and the eight stages are their inversion; Kotter presents the diagnosis first, and it is the more transferable half.

The order matters "usually", and concurrency is expected: all efforts end up "operating in multiple stages at once", and a large transformation contains smaller projects each running the whole sequence.
Complacency is the default condition and is systemic rather than a defect of individuals; nine specific sources are named, most of them measurement and feedback failures.

Urgency may legitimately be manufactured. Engineered crises, deliberately accepted unrealistic targets and permitted failures are all endorsed, with a stated preference for opportunity-based routes where they will work.
A guiding coalition is selected for position power, expertise, credibility and leadership; a coalition of managers only is said to guarantee failure; large egos and "snakes" are excluded outright.
A usable vision is "explained within five minutes" and gets a reaction showing "both understanding and interest".
The vision is undercommunicated by orders of magnitude, and inconsistent behaviour by senior people "overwhelms other forms of communication".
Visible inconsistencies that cannot be removed must be explained aloud rather than defended.
Empowerment is barrier removal across four named categories — structures, skills, systems, supervisors — with HR systems singled out.
Short-term wins are planned, not hoped for; they must be visible, unambiguous and clearly attributable, and they are also a test of the vision.
Wins are dangerous. Celebration is the mechanism by which resisters end change efforts.
Interdependence is why the process needs eight stages: "you have to change nearly everything".
Culture changes at the end, only after new behaviour has visibly produced better results and the link has been made explicit; succession and promotion decide whether it holds.
Management produces consistency and leadership produces change, and transformation is over-managed and under-led; but stage 6 in particular fails without competent management.
**Interviewing is skilled, asymmetric inquiry.** A conversational tone coexists with deliberate control of purpose, pacing, follow-up, and attention.
**Check the team's worldview at the door.** Externalize assumptions before fieldwork so they can be noticed without making confirmation the session's job.
**Study behavior and meaning together.** A sequence without rationale is incomplete; a stated rationale without observed context may be idealized.
**Reframe without abandoning the brief.** A deeper problem can extend the commissioned question, but the team remains accountable for the original decision need.
**Use the participant's context and language.** Artifacts, interruptions, social relations, terminology, and misperceptions are part of the evidence.
**Prepare to improvise.** Objectives, screening, a field guide, roles, logistics, consent, and equipment make responsible flexibility possible.
**Treat recruiting as research data.** Scarcity, ambiguity, and mismatched contexts can falsify assumptions about the population or workflow.
**Ask, show, enact, and make.** Demonstration, mapping, role-play, concepts, sorting, and homework expose different layers of a practice.
**Build rapport through attention.** Follow-ups, silence, body language, selective self-disclosure, and respect for social norms show that the participant matters.
**Silence is interpreted, not applied.** It can invite continuation, make room for thought, or signal confusion and distress depending on person and culture.
**Assume contradictions are intelligible.** Explore the missing distinction instead of accusing the participant or averaging the conflict away.
**Separate record from interpretation.** Notes, recordings, photographs, sketches, transcripts, highlights, and debriefs have different evidential roles.
**Analyze cases before extracting themes.** Preserve enough context to understand a participant, then synthesize across cases rather than collecting decontextualized quotes.
**Research impact is designed.** Stakeholder involvement, visible process, appropriate output forms, and an explicit chain from evidence to implication determine whether findings enter decisions.
**Three design principles:** provider-agnostic, zero friction, progressive disclosure.
**Three core types:** `EvalItem` (one conversation, split into query and response), `Evaluator` (scores items), `EvalResults` (aggregated pass/fail counts, per-item detail, portal links).
**Two evaluator tiers:** `LocalEvaluator` for inner-loop and CI smoke tests without API calls; `FoundryEvals` for cloud LLM-as-judge. **They can be mixed in one run.**
**`FoundryEvals` defaults to relevance, coherence and task adherence**, adding **tool call accuracy** automatically when tool definitions are present.

**Three split strategies:** **Last turn** (default; response quality at a point), **Full** (task completion and trajectory), **Per-turn** (fine-grained). Custom splitters accepted. **"How you split determines what you're evaluating."**
**Expected outputs** pair positionally with queries; **expected tool calls** can be specified separately.
**Pre-existing responses from logs can be evaluated without re-running the agent.**
**Repetitions** exist "to detect non-deterministic behavior".
**Workflow evaluation** extracts each sub-agent's interactions and evaluates them individually alongside the workflow's overall output.
**Agent behaviour evaluators:** `intent_resolution`, `task_adherence`, `task_completion`, `task_navigation_efficiency`.
**Tool usage evaluators:** `tool_call_accuracy`, `tool_selection`, `tool_input_accuracy`, `tool_output_utilization`, `tool_call_success`.
**Quality evaluators:** `coherence`, `fluency`, `relevance`, `groundedness`, `response_completeness`, `similarity`. **Safety evaluators:** `violence`, `sexual`, `self_harm`, `hate_unfairness`.
**`task_navigation_efficiency` takes `actions` and `expected_actions` and requires no model parameter** — the one deterministic agent-behaviour check.
**Customer Satisfaction uses six dimensions:** helpfulness, completeness, clarity, tone, resolution, adaptability.
**Output is pass/fail with a `reason`**, plus a numeric `score` for 1–5-scale evaluators; the documented example shows `tool_call_accuracy` 2 against threshold 3 failing.

**Data mapping:** `{{item.*}}` for dataset fields; `{{sample.output_items}}` for structured output including tool calls, required by the trajectory evaluators; `{{sample.output_text}}` for plain text.
Many evaluators are **preview**, and one consulted page is a superseded **classic** variant.
**The AI gateway "extends API Management's existing API gateway; it's not a separate offering."** Capability availability varies by service tier.

**Supported endpoint types:** OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses, Anthropic Messages (v2 tiers), Google Vertex AI; Foundry and non-Microsoft providers including Amazon Bedrock; remote MCP servers; A2A agent APIs; self-hosted models.
**Unified model API (preview):** multiple backends behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with automatic format translation and policy applied once.
**Five stated challenges:** authenticate and authorise; load balance; monitor and log; manage token usage and quotas across applications; enable developer self-service.

**Token limit policy:** TPM limits or quotas over hourly, daily, weekly, monthly or yearly periods; keyed on subscription key, originating IP, or an arbitrary policy expression; **prompt tokens can be precalculated at the gateway** to avoid backend calls that would exceed the limit; remaining tokens exposed to downstream policy.

**Semantic caching** compares "vector proximity of the prompt to prior requests"; requires Azure Managed Redis or a RediSearch-compatible external cache; implemented by the paired `llm-semantic-cache-store` and `llm-semantic-cache-lookup` policies over the Embeddings API.
**Scale units and regional gateways** scale the gateway. The docs explicitly warn this does not scale the AI backends, which must be deployed in the same regions.

**Security:** managed identities remove the need for API keys; OAuth via credential manager for apps and agents including MCP servers; `llm-content-safety` policy for prompt moderation via Azure AI Content Safety.
**Load balancing modes:** round-robin, weighted, priority-based, session-aware. Priority routing is recommended specifically to saturate PTU endpoints first.
**Circuit breaker** uses **dynamic trip duration from the backend's `Retry-After` header** rather than a fixed interval.
**`llm-emit-token-metric`** emits token metrics with custom dimensions for filtering in Azure Monitor; logging captures prompts, completions and token usage "for billing and auditing".
**Governance plane:** Azure API Center catalogue for APIs, MCP servers and skills; developer portals; policy toolkit; Copilot Studio connector.
**AI gateway in Microsoft Foundry is preview.**
Agent behaviour is an authored artifact, separated into four kinds — **instructions, prompts, agents and skills** — with distinct trees and distinct application rules.
**Authoring source, packaging manifest and generated output are separated**, and the generated tree is declared non-canonical.
**RPI separates Research, Plan, Implement, Review and Follow-up** as gated phases with explicit return paths, rather than as a narrative order.
**Durable on-disk state under stable identifiers replaces session memory as the authority** for what was researched, planned, implemented and reviewed.
**Execution completion and acceptance outcome are distinct results**, and a completed phase is not an accepted one.
Review is decomposed into orientation, lens, severity normalisation and risk-scaled depth, so that two reviewers produce comparable findings.

**Untrusted content is data, not authority:** fetched pages, documents, repositories, tool output and issue bodies may not issue instructions, and embedded instructions are reported rather than obeyed.
**An agent may not record a human's approval.** Human review is a stop condition, not a checkbox the workflow can satisfy for itself.
**A gate may be advisory or authoritative, and the difference is a property of the tier it runs in** rather than of the check itself.
**Regex-graded behavioural checks test output shape, not correctness**, and the repository says so in its own documentation.
Missing dependencies are made to produce setup failures rather than silent passes.
Telemetry is opt-in, local, and redacted by default, with verbatim capture behind a separate explicit opt-in.
**The existence of a control is not evidence that the control works**, and this corpus is the clearest available worked example of the distinction at scale.
**Three build paths by service model:** Foundry (PaaS), Copilot Studio (SaaS), GPUs and containers (IaaS). Selection criteria: **technical capabilities, timeline, control requirements.**
**Foundry agent types:** **prompt agents** (declarative, no agent compute) and **hosted agents** (your containerized code on managed container compute).

**Foundry setup options:** **basic** for rapid prototyping, which **lacks network isolation**; **standard** with public networking for enterprise controls or private networking for confidential workloads.
**Declarative agents:** individual use, Copilot's orchestrator and models only, **no proactive interaction**, Microsoft 365 channels, hosted in Microsoft 365.
**Custom engine agents:** complex workflows, individual or group use, **full orchestration and model choice**, **proactive triggering**, internal and external channels, flexible hosting.

**Six published triggers for custom engine agents:** custom orchestration; own or domain-specific or multimodal models; group productivity; integrating an existing assistant; availability outside Microsoft 365; proactive messaging.
**Orchestrator ownership differs by tool:** Copilot Studio's own; Teams AI Action Planner; bring-your-own for Agents SDK and Foundry.
**Language support differs:** Teams AI (C#, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python); Agents SDK (C#, JavaScript, Python); Foundry (Python, C#); Copilot Studio (not applicable).
**Only Teams SDK, Microsoft 365 Agents SDK and Foundry agents can be published to the Microsoft Commercial Store** via the Agents Toolkit.
**Copilot Studio is "designed for small-scale deployments, such as department-level solutions."**

**Copilot Studio's stated limits:** less fine-grained control over API calls, actions and response formatting; less integrated pro-dev tooling than Agents Toolkit; **Adaptive Cards schema 1.6 and earlier**; slower feature availability.
**Tools connect via the Tool catalog, MCP and OpenAPI specifications**, with Logic Apps and Functions for serverless automation.
**The options are explicitly not mutually exclusive** — components on different platforms compose through MCP.

**Two Foundry-to-Microsoft-365 integration paths:** direct publish, which auto-provisions Azure Bot Service and Entra ID; or an Agents Toolkit proxy app for custom logic, SSO and multi-environment deployment.
**Purview's four capability groups:** insights and analytics; ready-to-use prompt data-loss policies; data risk assessments for oversharing; compliance controls.
**The oversharing argument:** generative AI "amplifies the problem of oversharing data" by surfacing content that is "obsolete, over-permissioned, or lacking governance controls."
**Default data risk assessment runs weekly over the top 100 SharePoint sites**, and, once configured, the **top 100 Fabric workspaces**.
**Assessment detail is organised as Identify, Protect, Monitor.**

**Remediation options:** restrict access by label via DLP; SharePoint Restricted Content Discovery to exempt sites; auto-labelling for unlabelled sensitive files; retention policies deleting content unaccessed for three years.
**Item-level actions:** Resolve, Apply sensitivity label, Notify owner, Remove sharing link — the last flagged as disruptive and to be used sparingly.

**Stated limits:** 200,000 items per location; counts possibly inaccurate above 100,000 files per location; OneDrive unsupported for item-level scanning; maximum 10 SharePoint sites for item-level scanning.
**Stated latencies:** 24 hours for policy data; 48 hours for custom assessment results; 4-day delay on first default assessment; 30-day expiry on custom results.
**Without an explicit policy, Copilot in Fabric and Security Copilot audit the event but not the prompts and responses.**

**Activity explorer captures** activity type and user, timestamp, AI app category and app, app accessed in, sensitive information types, files referenced and sensitive files referenced; prompts and responses are permission-gated.
**Workload taxonomy:** Copilot experiences and agents; Enterprise AI apps; Other AI apps.
**Defender's AI BOM** covers "application components, data, and AI artifacts from code to cloud."
**Automatic continuous discovery across five services:** Azure OpenAI Service, Azure AI Foundry, Azure Machine Learning, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI.
**Dependency scanning** names TensorFlow, PyTorch and Langchain; covers IaC misconfigurations and container image vulnerabilities.
**Four IaC AI security checks:** private endpoints; restricted endpoints; managed identity; identity-based authentication.
**Attack path analysis** targets "toxic combinations", with grounding and fine-tuning named as the data-exposure moments.
**Named AI-native attacks:** prompt injection, wallet attacks, model theft, data poisoning, plus data breach and denial of service.
**From 1 July 2026, agent-level discovery and posture require a Microsoft Agent 365 licence.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: A substantial majority of learners will produce a disqualifying condition that a reviewer judges incapable of firing.
predictions.instrument: the review movement's binary judgement, collected per learner.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Answers to opening item 2 will be markedly less specific than answers to items 1, 3 and 4.
predictions.instrument: the five written answers, coded *specific* / *generic* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who used the agent to attack their own position will revise it more often than those who used it to elaborate.
predictions.instrument: the prompt record against the revision count. **If this fails, the session's claim that an agreeing instrument is unused has no support at this scale**, and the movement should be rewritten as an assertion rather than a demonstration.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-2 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3, added by the §4.3 amendment) will produce disqualifying conditions judged capable of firing more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the reviewer's binary judgement across two cohorts, one run before the amendment and one after — or, absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on whether exercise 3 was completed. **This is the session's only direct test of the mechanism §3.2 rests on**, and a null result would mean the amendment in §4.3 was ceremony.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of learners will accept at least one agent-produced claim about the platform without a citation, despite the instructions file requiring one in every sentence.
predictions.instrument: the learner's submitted feasibility check, coded for whether each platform claim carries a page reference and a date. **This predicts the failure of the session's own countermeasure**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners will report the platform check as the more useful half of the session and the opening items as the less useful, and the reverse will hold at [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) when the disqualifying condition is tested against a brief built to fire it.
predictions.instrument: a two-item preference question at the close of S001 and again at the close of S010. **This is a prediction about the gap between how learning feels and how it works**, and if it fails in the first half the session's opening is not doing what this paper claims.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: A majority of learners will place the generalisation decision inside their own accountability list before the session and outside it afterwards.
predictions.instrument: item 3's written answer against the corresponding line of the finished boundary statement, coded by a second reader as *inside* / *outside* / *unstated*.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Proposal lists will contain systematically less consequential items than accountability lists, judged by whether the learner would perform the item anyway.
predictions.instrument: exercise 2's binary judgement, collected per item rather than per learner, so that a single genuine concession is not masked by four decorative ones.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: A majority of learners will fail to produce a boundary violation in exercise 4, and will report the agent as compliant.
predictions.instrument: the submitted prompt record, coded for whether a violation was elicited and how many attempts were made. **This predicts the failure of the session's own countermeasure** — the green-check failure mode in §5 is countered by an instruction to try to break the boundary, and an instruction to attempt something is not the same as attempting it. If it holds, step 5 should become a supplied adversarial prompt rather than a learner-authored one.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Learners who receive the roadmap refusal will report lower confidence in their own judgement immediately after the movement and no lower confidence a week later, while learners who receive a quality-based refusal will show the reverse.
predictions.instrument: a single confidence item at the close of the movement and again at [S005](/wiki/seminars/S005.md), across a cohort split on the peer script. **This is the direct test of the tension §3.3 concedes**, and a sustained drop in the roadmap arm would mean the impersonal framing does not do the work this paper claims for it.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-3 answer against the criterion — exercise 3, added by the §4.3 amendment — will produce boundary lines that name a function and a threshold more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the reviewer's coding across two cohorts, one before the amendment and one after; absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on whether exercise 3 was completed. **This is the session's only direct test of the mechanism §3.2 rests on**, and a null result would mean the §4.3 amendment was ceremony.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: In a majority of learner environments, only one of the two boundary files will appear in the request payload, and learners will not notice until instructed to look.
predictions.instrument: the recorded payload observation, coded for which files appeared and whether the discrepancy was reported before step 4 or only after. **If both files appear reliably and learners notice unprompted, the session's central platform claim has no demonstration at this scale**, and the step should be rewritten around a deliberately misplaced file instead.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners will leave item 5 blank or answer it with a restatement of item 2.
predictions.instrument: the five written answers, coded *specific* / *generic* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Restatements written before the agent is invoked will share fewer nouns with the original request than restatements written afterwards.
predictions.instrument: a noun-overlap count between request and restatement, applied to a cohort split by sequencing.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: A substantial minority of learners will open the agent before committing their restatement, and will not report having done so.
predictions.instrument: file timestamps on the committed restatement against the first prompt in the session log. **This predicts the failure of the session's own countermeasure** — the commit-first rule is procedural and has no detector, and a rule whose violation rate is unmeasured is an assumption. If it holds, the rule should become a tool-enforced ordering rather than an instruction.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: A majority of first-attempt alternative sets will differ in configuration rather than in mechanism, despite the instructions file requiring otherwise, and the agent will not flag this about its own output.
predictions.instrument: the three alternatives, coded by a second reader as *distinct mechanisms* / *configurations of one*. **This is the second prediction of a countermeasure failing**, and it is included because an instruction an executor applies to itself is the weakest control in the session.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Learners will more often revise their restated problem category when at least one alternative is classified `NOT ADDRESSED` than when all three are classified `SUPPORTED`.
predictions.instrument: the documentation verdict table against whether the restated category differs from the request's category, judged by a second reader. **If this fails, the documentation check is doing no discovery work** and belongs at [S011](/wiki/seminars/S011.md) as an architecture exercise instead of here.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners who produce a datable occurrence will more often revise the problem category than learners who produce only a workaround.
predictions.instrument: the presence of a date in the artefact against whether the restated category differs from the request's, judged by a second reader. If this fails, the occurrence requirement is doing no diagnostic work and should be reduced to a recommendation.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: In the exercise 6 transcript coding, marks identifying a difficulty rather than a solution will cluster in the later half of the conversation.
predictions.instrument: position of each mark as a proportion of transcript length, aggregated across the cohort. **This tests a practitioner claim the corpus asserts and never measured**, and a null result would mean the buried-problem observation is folklore rather than a pattern.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most decision-rights columns will, before instruction, contain restatements of job titles rather than statements of what a person can settle alone.
predictions.instrument: the written item 1 answers, coded *title* / *right* / *mixed* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Pre-commitments written before exercise 6 will more often be judged externally unrecognisable than those revised after it.
predictions.instrument: the exercise's binary judgement, collected before and after revision.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who design a task-based probe will identify more absent decision rights than those who design a question-based one.
predictions.instrument: probe type against the count of stop-capable attendees identified, per learner. **If this fails, the indirect-probe requirement is decorative** and should become a recommendation rather than a standard.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: A majority of learners' step-1 answers and their post-step-3 answers will be identical, and those learners will report that the documentation confirmed what they already thought.
predictions.instrument: the timestamped step-1 sentence against the finished scope declaration, coded *changed* / *unchanged*. **This predicts the failure of the session's own countermeasure** — the workflow exists to disturb an assumed audience, and a learner who reads the page as confirmation has performed the lookup without performing the check.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Learners will report the scope-declaration exercise as more useful than the room reading immediately after the session, and the reverse at [S007](/wiki/seminars/S007.md), when the absent parties become the subject.
predictions.instrument: a two-item preference question at the close of each session. **This is a prediction about the gap between how learning feels and how it works**, and if the ordering does not reverse, objection 3's charge of false equivalence gains force.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Where a cohort debriefs a shared room reading, teams will converge on a conclusion while giving incompatible reasons for it, and the incompatibility will not be noticed unless reasons are written before discussion.
predictions.instrument: individual written reasons collected before the debrief, coded for compatibility, against the group's stated conclusion. **This is the session's only direct test of the §3.5 transfer**, and a null result would mean the assessor-cognition finding does not carry from portfolios to rooms.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first submissions will contain an assumption column that is empty or contains only trivial items.
predictions.instrument: the artefact's two columns, with each assumption coded *consequential* / *trivial* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Element 4 will fail more learners than any other element.
predictions.instrument: per-element failure counts across the cohort at first submission.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: A majority of context sections judged neutral by their authors will be judged predictive by a stranger who reads only that section.
predictions.instrument: the workflow's step-5 stranger test, run independently by an assessor on a sample, against the learner's own recorded judgement. **This predicts the failure of the session's own countermeasure** — the neutrality test is performed by the learner on their own writing, which is the weakest control in the design, and a rule whose self-application rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Learners with prior exposure to either product will produce build-path records with more `SUPPORTED` cells and fewer `NOT ADDRESSED` cells than learners with none, and will not more often pass element 6.
predictions.instrument: a self-reported prior-exposure item against the verdict distribution and the element-6 outcome. **This is the direct test of objection 3.** If prior exposure predicts element 6 outcomes, the element is assessing product knowledge and should be replaced.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Learners whose conditions were judged incapable of firing at [S001](/wiki/seminars/S001.md) will amend them before this assessment more often than they defend them.
predictions.instrument: the S001 review judgement matched against the presence of a dated amendment at S005. If this fails, the S001 review is not carrying forward and the amendment prompt should move earlier.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Assessors' written reasons will name the element that carried the judgement in a minority of cases at first use, and will converge on naming it after the reasons are read aloud in a moderation session.
predictions.instrument: the written reasons, coded for whether an element is named, before and after moderation. **This tests the §3.3 claim about substantiation making reasoning discussable**, and a failure would mean the written reason is ceremony and a mark would be cheaper.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Where two assessors independently judge the same defence, they will agree on the pass/fail outcome more often than they agree on which element carried it.
predictions.instrument: paired assessments on a sample, with outcome agreement and element agreement recorded separately. **This is the direct test of the transfer in §3.3** — convergence on an outcome concealing divergence in reasoning — and a null result would mean the finding does not carry from portfolio assessment to engineering defence.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first registers will attribute at least one frozen constraint to a document rather than to a person.
predictions.instrument: the source column, coded *person* / *document* / *consensus* per entry.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: The frozen list will shorten after the review movement in most cases, and the reduction will be larger for learners from long-lived estates.
predictions.instrument: frozen-entry counts before and after review, split by the learner's declared background.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who write a test they cannot run will more often carry the constraint unresolved into [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) than learners who write a test within their reach.
predictions.instrument: test feasibility coded at S006 against the constraint's status in the S010 artefact. **If this fails, the test column is recording intention rather than plan** and should require a named person able to answer.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Answers to opening item 4 will be markedly less concrete than answers to items 1, 2 and 3, and will name an intention rather than a discoverable fact.
predictions.instrument: the five written answers, coded *discoverable fact* / *intention* / *absent* by a second reader. **This is the prediction that the session's generation phase is aimed at the right item**, and if item 4 is answered as well as the others the material should be reordered.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of learners will record at least one instrument-derived entry with an empty or generic `blind_to` field, despite step 7 requiring blind spots to be written as entries.
predictions.instrument: the register's instrument blocks, coded for whether `blind_to` names a specific unscanned region. **This predicts the failure of the countermeasure added by the §4.5 amendment**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption wearing a fix's clothes.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-4 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce register entries whose tests a reviewer judges capable of settling the question more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: the reviewer's binary judgement across two cohorts, or absent two cohorts, a within-cohort split on whether exercise 3 was completed. **This is the session's only direct test of the mechanism §3.2 rests on**, and a null result would mean the comparison prompt is ceremony.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners will report the platform workflow as the more useful half of the session and the register as the less useful, and the reverse will hold at [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) when a refusal has to rest on a constraint that was actually established.
predictions.instrument: a two-item preference question at the close of S006 and again at the close of S010.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first maps will contain nobody who bears a cost and holds no purchasing authority.
predictions.instrument: the map's entries, coded *buyer* / *user* / *affected non-buyer* / *blocker* / *entitlement-only* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Objections judged straw by a reader who did not write them will be revised more often than those judged genuine, and the effect will be greater when read aloud than when read silently.
predictions.instrument: the read-aloud judgement against the presence of a revision, with a cohort split by reading mode.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who write a refusable ask will more often record a changed belief than learners whose ask admits only agreement.
predictions.instrument: the ask, coded *refusable* / *announcement*, against whether the artefact records a belief change after the staged decline. **If this fails, the refusability requirement is a stylistic preference** and should be dropped rather than defended.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Answers to the second half of opening item 4 — who is currently forbidden from reading the data — will be absent or generic in most cases, while answers to its first half will be specific.
predictions.instrument: the written answers, coded per half as *specific* / *generic* / *absent* by a second reader. **This is the prediction that the generation phase is aimed at the right item.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of enforcement rows will name a mechanism without naming a trust boundary, or will name the service as the boundary in designs where the application supplies the filter string.
predictions.instrument: the enforcement rows, coded for whether the stated boundary matches the described mechanism. **This predicts the failure of the countermeasure introduced by the §4.5 amendment**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners who complete workflow step 5 — chunking without projection — will name granularity as a verification concern in later sessions more often than those who read about it.
predictions.instrument: mentions of retrieval granularity in the [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) artefact, split by step-5 completion.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-4 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce enforcement rows judged complete more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a reviewer's four-part completeness judgement, split within cohort on exercise-3 completion. **A null result would mean the comparison prompt is ceremony**, and the same prediction is made at [WP-006](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-006.md) so a null in both would indict the pattern rather than the session.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first findings will state the simple option's failure as a property claim rather than as an observable event.
predictions.instrument: the stated failure, coded *observable* / *property claim* / *absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most estate columns will be empty or filled from memory rather than from anything the customer supplied.
predictions.instrument: the estate entries, coded by whether a source is named.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who found the agent's strengthening argument more persuasive than its undermining argument will revise their finding more often than those who found the reverse.
predictions.instrument: the learner's recorded judgement of the two agent outputs against the presence of a revision. **If this fails, the double-agent device demonstrates nothing about instrument use** and should be replaced by a written pair of cases produced by peers.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Most build-path comparisons will differ on fewer axes than the artefact provides, and the axis most often left identical across all three options will be initiation.
predictions.instrument: the completed comparison tables, coded for the number of axes on which the options actually differ.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of learners will complete a sufficiency finding without standing up the lexical baseline, and will nonetheless assert that a simpler retrieval approach would be insufficient.
predictions.instrument: presence of a reproducible baseline in the artefact, against the presence of an insufficiency claim about retrieval. **This predicts the failure of the countermeasure added at §4.4**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-4 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce observable failure statements more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a second reader's binary judgement, split within cohort on exercise-3 completion.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Findings that answer the composition check will more often recommend a mixed outcome — simple for one component, sophisticated for another — than findings produced before the §4.5 amendment.
predictions.instrument: the verdict form, coded *single* / *mixed*, across cohorts before and after the amendment. **A null result would mean the composition check is a field learners fill rather than a question they answer.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most first statements will contain a baseline figure with no named instrument.
predictions.instrument: the baseline field, coded *measured with instrument* / *asserted* / *declared absent* by a second reader.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Most attribution lines will name nobody, and most learners will record this as a finding only after the review movement.
predictions.instrument: the attribution field before and after review, coded *named* / *nobody, recorded* / *blank*.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who produced a do-nothing statement with a frequency and a bearer will produce fewer refusals at [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) than those whose statement was categorical.
predictions.instrument: the S009 artefact's form against the S010 decision. **If this fails, the session is not making refusal expensive**, which is its stated purpose, and the commitment made at [WP-001](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-001.md) is undischarged.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Most cost-of-proceeding entries will price the build and omit what is paid at rest, even among learners who completed the platform workflow.
predictions.instrument: the cost-of-proceeding block, coded for whether an idle-cost line is present and non-generic.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of personal-cost columns will be present but generic — naming discomfort rather than immediacy, certainty, a survivability asset and an alternative.
predictions.instrument: the learner's own column, coded against the four required properties. **This predicts the failure of the countermeasure added at §4.5**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners whose personal-cost column names at least one survivability asset will accept the sponsor's accommodation at [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) less often than those whose column names none.
predictions.instrument: the presence of a named asset at S009 against the sponsor's binary record of offer acceptance at S010. **This is the session's only test of whether pricing the refusal changes anything**, and a null result would mean the §4.5 amendment is bookkeeping.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners will not report increased reluctance to refuse after completing the personal-cost block, and any observed shift will be towards more specific rather than fewer refusals.
predictions.instrument: a single self-report item at the close of S009 and the refusal count at S010, compared against cohorts run before the amendment. **This is the direct test of §8's third objection, and it is the prediction this paper would least like to lose.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: A substantial share of learners will accept the sponsor's accommodation at first attempt.
predictions.instrument: the sponsor's binary record of whether the offer was accepted, collected per learner.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Conditions written at [S001](/wiki/seminars/S001.md) and judged capable of firing by the S001 reviewer will fire against Brief B more often than those judged incapable.
predictions.instrument: the S001 review judgement matched against element 1's outcome. **This is the closest thing the stage has to a check on its own opening session**, and a null result would mean the S001 review movement is not discriminating.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners whose do-nothing statement carried a frequency and a bearer will state the cost of the refusal in the customer's terms more often than those whose statement was categorical.
predictions.instrument: the S009 artefact's form against element 4's outcome.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Most learners will report the same trace scoring differently under different split strategies as the most surprising thing in the session, and most will have used the default strategy before being told to choose.
predictions.instrument: a single free-text item at the close, coded for whether the split-strategy demonstration is named; plus the configuration submitted, coded for whether the strategy was stated before results were seen.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of first evaluations will be controls rather than checks — safeguards that cannot fail without a person failing to act — despite element 7 requiring a measured disagreement rate.
predictions.instrument: the submitted evaluation, coded *check* / *control* / *mixed* by a second reader. **This predicts the failure of element 7's countermeasure**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners whose evaluation passes at their chosen threshold will withdraw or soften their refusal more often than learners whose evaluation fails, and in a minority of those cases a second reader will judge the withdrawal unwarranted.
predictions.instrument: the evaluation outcome against the delivered refusal's strength, with unwarranted withdrawals coded by a reader blind to the evaluation result. **This is the direct test of §8's fourth objection, and it is the prediction this paper would least like to lose.**

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners who hand-labelled their own traces will report a disagreement with the evaluator that surprises them, and will more often name a residual harm the check cannot reach.
predictions.instrument: the labelled batch, and element 7's not-covered statement coded *specific* / *generic* / *absent*.

predictions.label: Prediction 8.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-5 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 3) will produce evaluations judged to be checks rather than controls more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a second reader's binary judgement, split within cohort on exercise-3 completion. **The same prediction is made at [WP-006](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-006.md), [WP-007](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-007.md) and [WP-008](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-008.md), so a null across all four would indict the comparison pattern rather than any one session.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: A substantial majority of learners will initially state an output that has no failure state.
predictions.instrument: the opening item 3 answers, coded *observable* / *unobservable* / *absent* by a second reader before instruction.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: The strike-out review will remove lines from most first-draft charters, and the lines removed will concentrate on the stated output rather than on the people list.
predictions.instrument: the struck lines, coded by charter element, collected per learner. **If the review removes nothing, the charter format is already doing the work and the review movement is ceremonial.**

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who take the interleaving position will produce narrower necessary-people lists than those who take the concentrated-instrument position.
predictions.instrument: the named-authority count on each charter, against the position taken. **If the two are indistinguishable, the position paragraph is decorative and should be replaced by a direct question.**

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: The venue argument will be the most frequently omitted charter element.
predictions.instrument: presence or absence of a derived venue consequence, per submitted charter.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of first protocols will retain at least one question inviting the customer to endorse the practitioner's solution category, despite step 5 naming that class first.
predictions.instrument: the exported topics, coded *endorsement question present* / *absent* by a second reader. **This predicts the failure of step 5's countermeasure**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners who built a topic will follow their own question order more rigidly in the [S015](/wiki/seminars/S015.md) session than learners who did not, as judged by the number of unplanned follow-ups pursued.
predictions.instrument: the assessor's tally of pursued threads, split within cohort on whether a topic was exported. **This is the direct test of §8's third objection and it is the prediction this paper would least like to lose.**

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-5 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 4) will produce charters whose stated output names a currency more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a second reader's binary judgement, split within cohort on exercise-4 completion. **The same prediction is made at [WP-010](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-010.md), so a null across both would indict the comparison pattern rather than either session.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: On opening item 1, most learners will produce no condition marked *us*, and a larger majority will produce none marked *platform*.
predictions.instrument: the marked list, counted by scope per learner before instruction.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Stop positions written before the [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) comparison will be judged incapable of firing more often than those written after it.
predictions.instrument: the peer's binary judgement, collected at both points in the session.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who derived the closed loop themselves will identify the same structure at [S068](/wiki/seminars/S068.md) more often than those who were shown it.
predictions.instrument: unprompted identification at [S068](/wiki/seminars/S068.md), against a record of which route the learner took here. **This requires a deliberate split and the design does not currently create one, so the prediction is unmeasurable as the session stands.** That is recorded rather than fixed.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Waivers recorded during [S015](/wiki/seminars/S015.md) will more often lack a name than lack a reason.
predictions.instrument: the submitted gates, coded for presence of name and presence of reason.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of submitted gates will record a finding without a reproducible query, a read depth, or both — despite all three being required fields.
predictions.instrument: the platform-premise rows, coded for completeness by a second reader. **This predicts the failure of §8's third countermeasure**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: The silence field will be the most frequently empty field in the gate, and where completed will more often record a denial than an absence.
predictions.instrument: the silence entries, coded *absent* / *records an absence* / *records a denial* by a second reader. **If denials dominate, the session has taught learners to over-read documentation and the movement should be rewritten around a page that omits something obvious.**

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-2 count against the taught criterion (exercise 5) will submit gates containing a fixable inward condition more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a second reader's binary judgement, split within cohort on exercise-5 completion. **The same prediction is made at [WP-010](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-010.md) and [WP-011](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-011.md), so a null across all three would indict the comparison pattern rather than any one session.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: In the first drill round, most facilitators will supply at least one option, example or completion within their first three questions.
predictions.instrument: the observer's tally, collected per round.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Forbidden lists written before the first drill will be judged costless more often than those revised after it.
predictions.instrument: a peer's binary judgement on whether the list contains a move the author is inclined to make, collected at both points.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners will name the remote-participant owner less often than any other required field of the plan.
predictions.instrument: field-presence counts across submitted plans.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: The wellness amendment will most often be written as an addition to the plan rather than as a removal from it.
predictions.instrument: the amendments, coded *adds an activity* / *removes or bounds an activity*. **If additions dominate, the session has taught the learner to document the constraint rather than to obey it**, and the movement should be rewritten to require a removal.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Asked after the platform work what their constraint file established, a majority of learners will describe a property of their questions rather than a property of their questions' form.
predictions.instrument: a single free-text item, coded *shape* / *quality* / *conflated* by a second reader. **This predicts the failure of §8's third countermeasure**, and it is included because a countermeasure whose failure rate is unmeasured is an assumption.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: In step 6, the most common observed outcome will be that the constraint did not hold and nothing announced it.
predictions.instrument: the recorded outcome, coded *held and reported* / *held silently* / *did not hold*, per learner and per host-and-model pair. **If constraints hold reliably across hosts, the session's claim that enforceability is a property of the host rather than the file is wrong and §3.7 should be rewritten.**

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-4 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 5) will produce plans whose second field names a condition rather than an encouragement more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a second reader's binary judgement, split within cohort on exercise-5 completion. **The same prediction is made at [WP-010](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-010.md), [WP-011](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-011.md) and [WP-012](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-012.md), so a null across all four would indict the comparison pattern rather than any one session.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Most learners' first rehearsal record will describe the outcome before it names the prohibition.
predictions.instrument: the records, coded for which appears first.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: The sceptic and the unanswerable question will produce more prohibition breaches than the silent participant.
predictions.instrument: observer tallies by situation, aggregated across the cohort.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Learners who record a near-miss in rehearsal will self-report a breach at [S015](/wiki/seminars/S015.md) more often than those who record none.
predictions.instrument: the [S015](/wiki/seminars/S015.md) submissions, coded for self-recorded breach, against this session's records. **If self-recording does not carry forward, the near-miss field is producing a rehearsal artefact rather than a habit.**

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Asked what they would have to observe for the sceptic-becomes-advocate claim to be false, most learners will produce a condition that could not occur.
predictions.instrument: the written condition, judged for whether it could fire, by the same criterion used at [S001](/wiki/seminars/S001.md).

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of first escalation designs will route a well-formed disagreement to the same destination as an unparsed utterance.
predictions.instrument: the submitted designs, coded *two paths* / *three paths* by a second reader, against the step-5 write-up.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Learners who completed the escalation exercise will name the sceptic or the unanswerable question as their near-miss at [S015](/wiki/seminars/S015.md) more often than learners who did not.
predictions.instrument: the [S015](/wiki/seminars/S015.md) records, coded by named prohibition, split within cohort on completion of the platform work. **This is the direct test of §8's third objection, and it is the prediction this paper would least like to lose** — a null means the configuration exercise taught routing and nothing else.

predictions.label: Prediction 7.
predictions.claim: Learners instructed to compare their item-5 answer against the taught criterion (exercise 6) will name a specific prohibition and a later cost more often than learners who read the same material without the comparison prompt.
predictions.instrument: a second reader's binary judgement, split within cohort on exercise-6 completion. **The same prediction is made at [WP-010](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-010.md) through [WP-013](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-013.md), so a null across all of them would indict the comparison pattern rather than any one session.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Item 5 will be the most frequently failed specification item.
predictions.instrument: per-item pass rates across the cohort, reported without aggregation.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Candidates who stop on the unmet gate condition will be rarer than those who proceed with a named waiver, and both will be rarer than those who proceed with an unattributed one.
predictions.instrument: the submitted gates, coded three ways.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Closing records written before the debrief will contain more specific nouns than a matched set written after it.
predictions.instrument: a deliberate split in which half the cohort writes a second record after the debrief, compared blind by a second reader. **The design does not currently create that split, so the prediction is unmeasurable as the assessment stands.** Recorded rather than fixed.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Self-recorded prohibition breaches will exceed assessor-found ones.
predictions.instrument: the two counts. **If assessor-found breaches dominate, the honesty incentive in item 4 is not working and the item should be rewritten.**

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of specifications will contain at least one falsifier that names no reachable observer, and candidates will identify this themselves in exercise 4 more often than assessors identify it in the defence.
predictions.instrument: the falsifier entries, coded *observer named and reachable* / *observer named, unreachable* / *no observer*, by a second reader, against the exercise-4 self-assessment. **This predicts the failure of element 7's countermeasure.**

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Candidates with prior agent-configuration experience will not differ from those without on element 7's outcome, although they will differ on the time taken.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
